questions.stem:
Select the correct equation for the following problem:
Lilit has 324 stamps in her stamp collection. This is 4 times as many stamps as Bligh has in her collection. How many stamps does Bligh have? (Let Bligh have N stamps)
questions.hint: Lilit's total is equal to 4 times Bligh's total.
Subtract 4 from both sides, then multiply by 3.

questions.stem: Page numbers are printed using 9 single-digit numerals (pages 1–9), 180 digits for pages 10–99 and 2700 digits for pages 100–999. If 3425 digits are used in total, what is the last page number?
questions.hint: First count the digits used through page 999, then divide the remaining digits by 4.

keyPoints.note: Add the digit counts through page 999.

steps.explain: Find the remaining digits and number of four-digit page labels.

meta.sourcePaper: Sydney Grammar School Form I Mathematics Annual Examination 2017

questions.stem: Five people finish a race. Fred finishes first and Noel last. Alan is immediately behind Steve, and Bob finishes ahead of Steve. In what place does Bob finish?
questions.hint: Place Fred first and Noel fifth. Alan must be immediately after Steve, so find which two middle places fit Bob and Steve.

keyPoints.note: Steve’s place is one number before Alan’s.
Bob must be placed earlier than Steve.

steps.explain: Alan is immediately after Steve, so their possible pair is 3rd and 4th.
Bob must finish ahead of Steve; among the open places, that makes Bob 2nd.

meta.sourcePaper: Sydney Grammar School Year 7 Mathematics Task 3 (2013)

questions.stem: A meal consists of one choice from 2 dinners, 3 main meals and 2 desserts. How many different meals can be chosen?
questions.hint: For each dinner choice there are 3 main-meal choices, and each of those has 2 dessert choices. Multiply the independent choices.

keyPoints.note: Choose one item from each group.

steps.explain: Record the number of choices in each group.
Multiply because one choice is made from every group.

meta.sourcePaper: Sydney Grammar School Year 7 Mathematics Task 3 (2013)

questions.stem: The diagram shows four small squares made from 12 matches. Remove two matches so that exactly two squares remain. Draw your sample answer.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Remove two adjacent inner matches from the central cross (for example, the right-middle horizontal match and the bottom-middle vertical match). This leaves exactly two squares of different sizes: one large 2×2 outer square and one small 1×1 corner square, with no loose ends.
questions.hint: The remaining squares do not have to be the same size. Consider keeping the large 2×2 outer square intact while keeping one small 1×1 corner square.

keyPoints.note: Remove two adjacent matches from the inner cross.
One large 2×2 square and one small 1×1 square (no loose/dangling matches).

steps.explain: Start with the 2-by-2 grid. There are 12 matches forming four 1×1 squares and one 2×2 outer square (total of 5 squares).

steps.explain: The 8 outer matches remain closed forming 1 large 2×2 square, and the remaining 2 inner matches complete 1 small 1×1 square. Exactly 2 squares remain with no loose ends.
